title: FCC Commissioner Gomez to Speak at LPTV Day at 2026 NAB Show
body_html:
Understanding the Infrastructure Implications

The announcement of FCC Commissioner Gomez speaking at LPTV Day at the 2026 NAB Show may seem like a straightforward news item, but it touches on a critical aspect of broadcast infrastructure: signal routing and transport. At the heart of this infrastructure is the ST 2110 or SDI fabric that connects cameras, production switchers, graphics engines, and distribution paths. The reliability and efficiency of this fabric are crucial to the overall quality of the broadcast. As engineering leads consider the implications of this announcement, they must map it against real workflows to understand the potential impact on cost, throughput, reliability, and editorial speed. The ST 2110 standard, in particular, plays a vital role in the transport of audio and video signals over IP networks. Its adoption has been driven by the need for greater flexibility, scalability, and interoperability in broadcast systems. By using ST 2110, broadcasters can take advantage of the benefits of IP-based infrastructure, such as reduced cabling and increased ease of signal routing. However, this also introduces new challenges, such as ensuring accurate timing and synchronization across the network. The use of PTP/IEEE 1588 timing protocols is essential in this regard, as it enables the precise synchronization of clocks across the network, ensuring that all devices are working in tandem.

Technical Breakdown and Workflow Implications

In a typical broadcast workflow, the signal routing and transport infrastructure is critical to the smooth operation of live production and playout control. The use of ST 2110 and SDI fabrics enables the efficient transport of signals between different devices, such as cameras, production switchers, and graphics engines. The integration of these devices is facilitated by protocols such as NMOS, which provides a standardized way of discovering and controlling devices on the network. By using NMOS, broadcasters can simplify the process of setting up and configuring their systems, reducing the risk of errors and downtime. The migration from SDI to IP-based infrastructure is a significant trend in the broadcast industry, driven by the need for greater flexibility and scalability. However, this migration also introduces new challenges, such as ensuring signal integrity and multivendor interoperability. The use of hybrid SDI/IP designs can help to mitigate these challenges, by enabling the integration of both SDI and IP-based devices into a single system. This approach allows broadcasters to take advantage of the benefits of IP-based infrastructure, while also ensuring that they can continue to use their existing SDI-based equipment.

Operational Impact and ROI

The adoption of ST 2110 and IP-based infrastructure can have a significant impact on the operational efficiency of a broadcast organization. By reducing the complexity of signal routing and transport, broadcasters can simplify their workflows and reduce the risk of errors and downtime. This can lead to significant cost savings, as well as improved reliability and quality of service. Additionally, the use of IP-based infrastructure can enable new business models and revenue streams, such as the delivery of live and on-demand content over the internet. The use of hybrid SDI/IP designs can also help to mitigate the challenges associated with the migration from SDI to IP-based infrastructure. By enabling the integration of both SDI and IP-based devices into a single system, broadcasters can take advantage of the benefits of IP-based infrastructure, while also ensuring that they can continue to use their existing SDI-based equipment. This approach can help to reduce the risk of errors and downtime, as well as minimize the disruption to existing workflows.

Challenges and Limitations

Despite the benefits of ST 2110 and IP-based infrastructure, there are still significant challenges and limitations to be addressed. One of the main challenges is ensuring signal integrity and multivendor interoperability, particularly in hybrid SDI/IP environments. This requires careful planning and configuration of the system, as well as the use of standardized protocols such as NMOS. Additionally, the migration from SDI to IP-based infrastructure can be complex and time-consuming, requiring significant investment in new equipment and training. The use of PTP/IEEE 1588 timing protocols is also critical to ensuring the accurate synchronization of clocks across the network. However, this can be challenging in environments where there are multiple devices and systems, each with their own clocking requirements. The use of specialized timing equipment, such as grandmaster clocks, can help to mitigate these challenges, but this can add complexity and cost to the system.

Strategic Implications and Future Directions

The adoption of ST 2110 and IP-based infrastructure is a significant trend in the broadcast industry, driven by the need for greater flexibility, scalability, and interoperability. As broadcasters continue to migrate from SDI to IP-based infrastructure, they will need to address the challenges and limitations associated with this transition. This will require careful planning and configuration of their systems, as well as the use of standardized protocols such as NMOS. The use of hybrid SDI/IP designs can help to mitigate the challenges associated with this migration, by enabling the integration of both SDI and IP-based devices into a single system. This approach can help to reduce the risk of errors and downtime, as well as minimize the disruption to existing workflows. As the broadcast industry continues to evolve, it is likely that we will see further adoption of IP-based infrastructure, as well as the development of new technologies and standards to support this transition.
